accroche: If you really were a brain hooked up to a computer, Putnam argues, you couldn't even say so.
contenu_vulgarise:
A brain floats in a vat of nutrient liquid, connected by its nerve endings to a computer so sophisticated that it simulates, impulse by impulse, an entire life: a body, a street, a job, a familiar face. Nothing, from the inside, makes it possible to tell this simulated existence from a real one. The scenario, popularized much later by the film *Matrix* in 1999, is formulated in these terms by the American philosopher Hilary Putnam in 1981, in his book *Reason, Truth and History*.

## An Argument, Not a Doubt

Descartes, as early as 1641 in the *Méditations métaphysiques* (Meditations on First Philosophy), had already imagined an evil genius capable of deceiving the senses entirely. Putnam takes up this worry, but does not try to prove, by observation, that we are not that brain: no observation could. He builds instead an argument about language. A word refers to something, he says, only through a real causal chain linking the speaker to the thing referred to, a history, not a mere resemblance: an ant that happens to trace in the sand a line resembling Winston Churchill has not drawn Churchill, having no connection to him whatsoever. Now a brain in a vat, if it really existed, would only ever have been in contact with electronic impulses and the simulated universe they compose. Its word “vat,” uttered in that world, could therefore refer only to the vat-in-the-simulation, never to the real vat in which its body actually floats.

## What It Shifts

The conclusion overturns the intuition ordinarily attributed to this kind of thought experiment. If a brain in a vat uttered the sentence “I am a brain in a vat,” that sentence would be false, since its words could refer only to the inside of the simulation, never to the real situation it claims to describe. In other words, the hypothesis destroys itself as soon as one tries to state it from the inside: it can be true only when said by someone who is precisely not in that situation. This is not an empirical guarantee about the world, Putnam claims to know nothing more than before about what really exists; it is a result about what language can and cannot accomplish. He himself writes that it took him several years to convince himself that the argument, however strange it may first seem, really holds up.

citation.texte: Although the people in that possible world can think and 'say' any words we can think and say, they cannot (I claim) refer to what we can refer to. In particular, they cannot think or say that they are brains in a vat (even by thinking 'we are brains in a vat').
citation.source: Reason, Truth and History, Cambridge University Press, 1981, ch. 1, “Brains in a Vat,” p. 8

carte.punch: If you were a brain in a vat, says Putnam, you couldn't even say so.
carte.idee: In 1981, Hilary Putnam argues that a brain in a vat could never refer to the real vat, having no causal link to it. Its sentence “I am a brain in a vat” would therefore be false the moment it uttered it: the hypothesis destroys itself.

quiz.question: Why, according to Putnam, could a brain in a vat not truthfully say that it is a brain in a vat?
choix: Because its words can refer only to what it has a real causal link with, that is, the simulation, never the real vat
Because the computer simulating it would technically prevent it from formulating this sentence
Because a brain without a body cannot, by definition, produce any thought
Because the question makes sense only if asked aloud, and a brain in a vat has no voice
quiz.explication: Nothing technically or logically prevents the brain from forming the sentence, and the lack of a body or a voice is not the obstacle: Putnam relies on the causal theory of reference, according to which a word refers to a thing only through a real causal link with it, a link the simulated brain has never had with the real vat.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Long before Putnam, which philosopher had already imagined a similar skeptical scenario, with an evil genius capable of deceiving the senses entirely?
choix: John Locke, in 1690
David Hume, in 1748
René Descartes, in 1641
Immanuel Kant, in 1781
quiz_supplementaire.explication: As early as 1641, in the *Méditations métaphysiques*, Descartes had already imagined an evil genius capable of deceiving the senses entirely, a worry that Putnam takes up in 1981 before turning it into an argument about language.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the example of the ant that happens to trace in the sand a line resembling Winston Churchill show?
choix: That mere resemblance is not enough to refer to something; a real causal link is needed
That chance can produce works as valid as a conscious intention
That Winston Churchill is recognizable even in an abstract line
That ants follow paths that sometimes reproduce complex shapes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For Putnam, a word or an image refers to a thing only through a real causal chain linking them, a history, never a mere accidental resemblance, like that of the ant's line with Churchill.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which film, released well after Putnam's text, popularized this scenario of the brain hooked up to a computer?
choix: Blade Runner, in 1982
Matrix, in 1999
Inception, in 2010
eXistenZ, in 1999
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card specifies that the brain-in-a-vat scenario, formulated by Putnam in 1981, was popularized much later by the film Matrix, released in 1999.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Putnam himself say, according to the card, about the argument he built?
choix: That he abandoned it after the book's publication, judging it too fragile
That he borrowed it almost entirely from Descartes without modifying it
That it applies only to worlds simulated by computer, not to dreams
That it took him several years to convince himself that it really holds up
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card reports that Putnam himself writes that it took him several years to convince himself that his argument, however strange it may first seem, really holds up.
